content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends supplementing the standard four-symptom tuberculosis (TB) screening tool with additional diagnostic methods to improve accuracy. Among individuals living with HIV who are not receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), C-reactive protein (CRP) testing has been identified as the most accurate supplementary tool. When used after a positive four-symptom screen, a CRP level above 5 mg/L demonstrated similar sensitivity (84%, 95% CI: 73–90%) to the four-symptom screen alone but significantly higher specificity (64%, 95% CI: 55–72%). Chest X-rays, when combined with the four-symptom screen in a parallel approach (where a positive result from either test prompts further diagnostic confirmation), showed the highest sensitivity (85%, 95% CI: 69–94%) for TB screening among outpatients on ART, compared to the four-symptom screen alone (53%, 95% CI: 36–69%). Studies evaluating computer-aided detection (CAD) software for chest X-rays revealed variability in accuracy among human readers and CAD systems. However, overlapping confidence intervals suggest minimal differences in diagnostic performance. Limited data exist on the use of CAD for chest X-rays in people living with HIV, and further research is needed to optimize its application in this population. Diagnosing TB in people living with HIV is challenging due to atypical clinical presentations, particularly in those with advanced disease. WHO recommends bacteriological testing for all individuals with TB symptoms. Molecular rapid diagnostic tests (molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests, or mWRDs) are preferred as initial diagnostic tools over smear microscopy or culture. These tests detect TB and rifampicin resistance and are recommended for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB. The Xpert® MTB/RIF and Xpert® MTB/RIF Ultra tests are particularly sensitive for people living with HIV, though the latter has slightly lower specificity due to trace results, which may indicate non-viable TB DNA in previously treated individuals. The lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) test, performed on urine samples, is an add-on diagnostic tool for people living with HIV, especially those with advanced disease or low CD4 counts. It is part of the standard care package for advanced HIV disease and has been shown to predict mortality and save lives when used alongside effective treatment. WHO also recommends the use of moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for TB diagnosis. These tests, which include products like Abbott RealTime MTB and Roche COBAS® MTB assays, are suitable for high-throughput settings and can detect resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid. However, they require laboratory infrastructure and reliable specimen transport systems. For TB screening among people living with HIV, WHO advises using molecular rapid diagnostic tests as an upfront diagnostic tool in high TB burden settings, particularly for hospitalized patients. In outpatient settings with TB prevalence exceeding 10%, molecular tests may also be used for screening, but positive results should be followed by confirmatory diagnostic assessments to avoid overtreatment. Extrapulmonary TB is more common in people living with HIV, particularly those with low CD4 counts. Common forms include lymph node TB, pleural TB, and disseminated TB, while pericardial and meningeal TB are less frequent but more likely to result in fatal outcomes. Diagnosing extrapulmonary TB is difficult due to the low sensitivity of smear microscopy and challenges in obtaining samples. Molecular rapid diagnostic tests are preferred for cerebrospinal fluid in suspected TB meningitis and for lymph node biopsies or fine-needle aspirations in suspected lymphadenitis. LF-LAM testing may also assist in diagnosis for individuals with low CD4 counts. Early initiation of ART is critical for reducing mortality in people with both TB and HIV. For drug-sensitive TB, the standard six-month regimen remains the primary treatment, but a shorter four-month rifapentine-based regimen has been shown to be equally effective and well-tolerated. This shorter regimen may be preferable for many patients and health systems, provided the cost and availability of rifapentine are addressed. For multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), which is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, treatment outcomes are poorer, particularly among people living with HIV. WHO recommends ART for all individuals with HIV, including those with MDR-TB, to improve clinical outcomes. Further research is needed to optimize the management of TB and HIV co-infection, particularly in resource-limited settings.
